headline: Approved tobacco mapping and quarterly reports, Community Health Link updates, and a report on Temporary Protected Status impacts.
summary: Members reviewed tobacco regulations, a communicable disease update, SAPHE 2.0 performance standards, inspection data, and the Community Health Link closing. They asked for updates on the Community Health Link transition and a report on Temporary Protected Status impacts. They also agreed to add the Civilian Review Board to the next agenda.
decisions: Approved the June 1 meeting minutes by unanimous roll call vote.
Approved the proposed amendments to the July 13, 2026 public hearing minutes by unanimous roll call vote.
Approved the July 13, 2026 public hearing minutes as amended by unanimous roll call vote.
Approved supporting development of mapping resources and quarterly reports related to the Tobacco Ordinance, by unanimous roll call vote with four in favor.
Approved receiving updates on the Community Health Link transition and inviting its leadership to a future meeting, by unanimous vote.
Approved a future report from Commissioner Seema Dixit on the City’s planning and response to Temporary Protected Status changes, by unanimous vote.
Approved adding a discussion of the Civilian Review Board to the next meeting agenda, 4-0.
Approved staff communicating with the City Manager about the Board’s interest in engaging the Human Rights Commission on the Civilian Review Board, by unanimous vote.

decision_evidence.quote: Michael Perotto made a motion to approve the June 1 BOH minutes. This was approved unanimously by roll call vote, with Frances Anthes, Joseph Kahoro, Patrick Lowe, and Michael Perotto voting in the affirmative.
Patrick Lowe made a motion to approve the proposed amendments to the minutes. It was approved unanimously by roll call vote.
Patrick Lowe made a motion to approve the public hearing minutes as amended. It was approved unanimously by roll call vote.

Michael Perotto moved to support the development of mapping resources and quarterly reports related to the Tobacco Ordinance. The motion was approved unanimously by roll call vote, with Joseph Kahoro, Michael Perotto, Patrick Lowe, and Chair Frances Anthes voting in favor.

Michael Perotto moved that the Board receive updates on the status and transition of Community Health Link (CHL) and invite CHL leadership to a future Board meeting to discuss the transition, continuity of services, and its impact on clients and staff. The motion was approved by a unanimous vote.

Dr. Lowe moved that Commissioner Seema Dixit, in collaboration with City administration and community partners, provide a future report to the BOH on the City’s planning and response to potential community and public health impacts associated with changes to Temporary Protected Status (TPS). ... It was unanimously approved by the Board.
Fran made a motion to include a discussion of the Civilian Review Board as an agenda item for the next Board meeting. The motion was approved unanimously with a (4–0).

The Chair moved that staff communicate with the City Manager to inform the Administration of the Board’s interest in engaging with the Human Rights Commission regarding the Civilian Review Board. The discussion would provide perspectives from other city boards and commissions as the Board revisits its prior position. The motion was unanimously approved.

WORCESTER BOARD OF HEALTH MEETING 
Meeting Minutes 
August 3, 2026 
25 MEADE STREET, ROOM 109 1ST FLOOR. WORCESTER, MA 
 
 
Welcome 
 
Board Members Present:  
Chair-Frances Anthes, Michael Perotto, Dr. Patrick Lowe, Joseph Kahoro 
 
Staff Present:  
Seema Dixit, HHS Commissioner; Jennifer Bradford, Medical Director, HHS; Lee Hall, Director 
of Housing and Inspectional Services; Nick Antanavica, Commissioner of Inspectional Services ; 
Cherry Tangri, Grant Manager; Amelia Houghton, Chief of Public Health Nursing; Kyle OConnor, 
Tobacco Prevention Specialist. 
 
Staff Virtual:  
Desiree Sutton, Business Manager ; Jennifer Nakijoba, Chief o f Community Health ; Brenda 
Wright, Principal Clerk  
 
Guest Present: 
Henry Schwan, Reporter- Worcester T&G  
 
1. Call to Order 
Chair Frances Anthes called the meeting to order at 6:30pm. 
2. Welcome and Introductions 
Board members introduced themselves: Michael Perotto, Patrick Lowe, Joseph Kahoro, and Chair 
Frances Anthes. Attendees present and virtual were also asked to introduce themselves 
3. Announcements 
The Chair reported that there were two sets of minutes to be approved: The last BOH minutes from 
June 1st BOH meeting and July 13th Tobacco Public Hearing. 
 
4. Minutes of last meeting 
The Chair called for a motion to approve the minutes presented. 
 
Michael Perotto m ade a motion  to approve the June 1 BOH minutes. This was  approved 
unanimously by roll call vote, with Frances Anthes, Joseph Kahoro, Patrick Lowe, and Michael 
Perotto voting in the affirmative.
The Board then reviewed the minutes of the July 13, 2026 public hearing on the proposed tobacco 
regulations. Chair Anthes recommended the following amendments: 
• Under the Summary of Written Public Comments, Item No. 2, removal of a repetitive 
sentence beginning, “The commentator also stated.” 
• Under Item No. 3, insertion of the word “some” to reflect that Meryl’s Safe Haven 
expressed some support for the proposed regulations. 
• On page six, within comments made by Cheryl Sbarra, Executive Director of the 
Massachusetts Association of Health Boards, addition of the word “unfavorably” to clarify 
that Worcester’s number of smoking establishments was being compared unfavorably with 
other Massachusetts communities. 
The Chair requested a motion to approve the proposed amendments to minutes.  
 
Patrick Lowe made a motion to approve the proposed amendments to the minutes.  It was approved 
unanimously by roll call vote.  
 
Fran then requested a motion to approve the public hearing minutes as amended.  
 
Patrick Lowe made a motion to approve the public hearing minutes as amended. It was approved 
unanimously by roll call vote. 
 
5. Nursing and Communicable Disease Update: Amelia Houghton, Chief PHN, DPH 
 
• Amelia provided a brief overview of the report distributed in advance and noted that Dr. 
Jennifer Bradford would provide additional information on the current cyclosporiasis 
outbreak. 
• Chair Anthes asked about increased West Nile virus activity. Amelia reported that 
Worcester’s risk level had increased to moderate, with 57 positive mosquito samples 
reported in the region during the week. 
• She noted that the increase is typical for this time of year, particularly following heavy 
rainfall, and confirmed that mosquito surveillance, control, and spraying activities are 
ongoing. 
• Public health recommendations included avoiding outdoor exposure at dawn and dusk, 
using mosquito repellent, treating clothing with insect repellent, and wearing protective 
clothing. 
• Amelia clarified that the positive mosquito samples do not represent human cases. No 
human cases of West Nile virus have been reported at this time. 
 
Dr. Jennifer Bradford Report 
• Dr. Jennifer Bradford provided an overview of cyclospora and cyclosporiasis, noting that 
cases typically increase from May through August. 
• She reported that the current outbreak is primarily affecting Midwestern states, with 
approximately 18 cases reported in Massachusetts, consistent with seasonal levels. Lettuce 
has been identified as a potential source.
• Dr. Bradford advised residents to thoroughly wash fresh produce and hands before 
handling food.  Symptoms may include diarrhea, nausea, loss of appetite, weight loss, 
abdominal cramping, and bloating. She advised those experiencing persistent or severe 
diarrhea to consult a healthcare provider. 
 
Michael Perotto asked whether certain areas of the city had higher levels of positive mosquito 
samples. Amelia advised that this information is available through the arbovirus reports and maps 
and agreed to distribute the weekly reports to Board members. 
 
Additional information may be accessed online at:  
Fight the Bite | City of Worcester and Mosquitoes and Ticks | Mass.gov  
https://www.mass.gov/mosquitoes-and-ticks  
https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/investigation.html  
https://www.fda.gov/food/outbreaks-foodborne-illness/outbreak-investigation-salmonella-eggs-
july-2026   
or by scanning the QR Codes below. 
       
    Cyclosporiasis Andes virus–related cluster.      Ebola Updates                                                                                          
 
The report can be accessed online at www.worcesterma.gov/public-health.The Board thanked 
Amelia and Dr. Bradford for their updates. 
 
6. Tobacco Update – Kyle OConnor, Tobacco Prevention Specialist, WDPH 
 
• Kyle O’Connor provided an update on tobacco regulations, permits, retail education, and 
enforcement. 
• He reported that updated tobacco regulations were approved July 13, 2026, and became 
effective July 15, 2026. One new tobacco sales permit has since been approved under the 
three-year grandfather provision. 
• There are currently 221 permitted tobacco retailers: 12 smoking bars, 22 smoke shops, and 
187 general retailers. The caps of 235 retailers and 15 smoking bars have not been reached. 
• Retail education and enforcement activities are ongoing, including youth compliance 
checks and educational visits regarding the updated regulations. 
 
 Patrick Lowe requested an overview of retail education visits and youth compliance checks. 
 
Mr. O’Connor explained that, 
- All tobacco retailers will receive education visits covering updated local and state 
regulations, retailer responsibilities, and employee training record requirements. 
- Education visits are ongoing and will take time to complete due to the number of retailers.
- Youth compliance checks are conducted at non-smoking tobacco retailers at least annually. 
Failed checks may result in fines or suspensions under the updated regulations. 
- Smoking bars are subject to additional compliance requirements and are addressed in 
coordination with state and local Police.  
 
The Board expressed appreciation to Kyle and the Division for the significant work completed in 
revising the tobacco regulations. They acknowledged the extensive process involved and noted 
that the updated regulations are intended to be clearer, more concise, and easier to implement. 
 
Dr. Lowe suggested developing a tobacco regulation dashboard to provide ongoing transparency 
on licensing, approvals, transfers, violations, and enforcement. He recommended periodic Board 
presentations and potential public access through the Division’s website. 
 
Kyle responded that the Division is developing dashboards covering inspections, enforcement, 
community engagement, policy updates, and retailer information. The Board discussed using 
mapping to show retailer locations, clustering, and 500 -foot buffer requirements. He agreed that 
mapping could help prospective retailers understand location requirements and said he’d bring the 
suggestion back to the team for consideration 
 
Motion – Tobacco Regulation Dashboard and Quarterly Reports 
The Board discussed formalizing a request for quarterly tobacco regulation reports, consistent with 
reporting from other divisions. Reports would include licensing activity, mapping, enforcement, 
and other implementation updates. 
 
Michael Perotto moved to support the development of mapping resources and quarterly reports 
related to the Tobacco Ordinance. The motion was approved unanimously by roll call vote, with 
Joseph Kahoro, Michael Perotto, Patrick Lowe, and Chair Frances Anthes voting in favor. 
 
Chair Anthes noted that the tobacco reports will be incorporated into the Board’s quarterly 
reporting structure and thanked Mr. O’Connor for his work. 
 
7. Presentation SAPHE 2.0: Presented by Cherry Tangri , Grant Manager for the Public 
Health Excellence Capacity Building Grant and Nick Antanavica, ISD Commissioner  
 
Before the presentation, the Chair thanked staff for the background guidance document and noted 
that several Board members had joined since the program’s implementation approximately one 
year ago. Cherry, who leads the SAPHE 2.0 reporting process, explaine d that SAPHE 2.0 (State 
Action for Public Health Excellence) is a collaborative initiative between the Inspectional Services 
Department (ISD) and the Division of Public Health (DPH). 
 
There was a brief delay at the start of the presentation due to technical difficulties with screen 
sharing. Once resolved, the presentation proceeded. 
• Cherry Tangri explained that legislation signed in November 2024 made annual Blueprint 
for Public Health Excellence performance standards reporting mandatory for all 351 
Massachusetts municipalities. She provided a brief history of the Blueprint, noting th at a
special legislative commission was established in 2016 to evaluate the effectiveness and 
efficiency of local public health systems. In 2019, the commission issued recommendations 
in six areas: workforce development, data, performance standards, capacity bu ilding, 
sustainable funding, and cross-jurisdictional services. She also reviewed state public health 
grant programs, noting that the current Capacity Building Grant supports larger 
municipalities, including Worcester. 
 
• She outlined performance standards for Boards of Health, including inspections, tobacco 
enforcement, environmental health, housing, food, pools, beaches, body art, epidemiology, 
and communicable disease investigations. Workforce standards address staff and Board 
training and credentials. 
 
• Cherry said that Worcester has completed both required surveys and is following annual 
reporting requirements. The standards also help assess capacity, identify service gaps, and 
guide improvements.  Cherry reviewed the Performance Standards Summary, which 
consolidates SAPHE 2.0 survey results across eight public health subject areas. The survey 
included 164 questions, with 151 applicable to Worcester. “Yes” responses indicated 
compliance, while “No” r esponses identified gaps and barriers such as staffing, training, 
funding, or lack of awareness. The results will help prioritize areas for improvement. 
Board discussion on presentation 
Board member Patrick Lowe requested clarification on the SAPHE 2.0 survey methodology. Ms. 
Tangri explained that the 164-question survey, with 151 applicable to Worcester, was completed 
collaboratively by subject matter experts and team leaders from DPH and ISD. Responses reflected 
staff consensus for each program area. The summary identified standards met and areas needing 
improvement, based on input from the respective program managers. 
HHS Commissioner Seema Dixit clarified that questions for each subject area were answered by 
the respective program experts and reflected the work and practices of those areas. She said the 
survey is meant to assess Worcester’s public health capacity, staffing, training, and resources 
rather than simply determine compliance.  She noted that the survey provides a consensus -based 
assessment that can help identify areas where additional state support is needed.  Seema said that 
these findings will be discussed with the Massachusetts Department of Public Health 
Commissioner in September. 
Cherry added that the survey also serves as a structured self-assessment that enables municipalities 
to identify operational strengths and gaps while informing requests for technical assistance and 
support from the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. She explained that a response 
indicating a need for improvement does not mean the Division has failed to perform a function or 
is non-compliant.  She said similar assessment efforts have been conducted nationally , and that 
Massachusetts has implemented SAPHE 2.0 as a structured approach to evaluating and supporting 
local public health capacity. The reporting period for the survey covered the previous fiscal year, 
July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.
The Chair asked whether the SAPHE 2.0 assessment now evaluates Worcester independently, 
noting its previous participation in a regional public health structure. Cherry confirmed that the 
current assessment focuses on Worcester’s local public health capacity and performance standards. 
The presentation can be accessed online at www.worcesterma.gov/public-health 
8. Inspectional Services Update: Nicholas Antanavica, ISD Commissioner 
 
SAFE 2.0 Data Tracking and Inspection Activity Report 
 
➢ Nick provided an update on public health activity tracking  in coordination with SAPHE 
2.0. In collaboration with DPH support, health inspectors began using digital daily tracking 
sheets in January to document inspection activities. He presented first- and second-quarter 
results, noting that the data will support reporting, compliance, training, and identification 
of Worcester-specific public health trends. 
 
➢ He presented housing inspection data, including inspection categories, complaints, and 
outcomes. More than 4,000 inspections were completed during the first two quarters, 
resulting in approximately 6,300 category placements. Common issues included nuisance  
conditions, particularly trash and overgrowth. Staff are refining the data presentation to 
account for duplicate entries and multiple violations. 
➢ Nick noted that collecting and analyzing inspection data will support data-driven decisions, 
policy development, and presentations to the Board and City Council. He also discussed 
developing heat maps to identify geographic trends and target outreach, education, grants, 
and resources to areas with identified needs. 
➢ Nick explained that the inspection data will establish a baseline as the City transitions to a 
risk-based inspection program. The data will help evaluate inspections, complaint trends, 
response methods, and enforcement strategies. He also reviewed air, water, and hazardous 
waste inspection data, highlighting seasonal trends such as beach and summer camp 
inspections, water testing, and increased sewer and discharge issues following heavy 
rainfall. 
 
The Chair expressed appreciation to Nick for the report 
 
Board questions/comments on presentation 
1. Michael Perotto asked about the timeline for addressing trash and nuisance complaints, using 
an overflowing dumpster as an example. Nick explained that while complex cases may take 
six to nine months, most are resolved sooner, typically within approximately three months. 
 
2. Patrick Lowe highlighted the value of distinguishing routine from complaint -driven 
inspections. He noted that analyzing and mapping the data could support a more proactive 
approach to public health and inform decision-making in areas such as tobacco regulation. He 
expressed appreciation for the development of the data system.
3. Fran asked whether the inspection data provided a baseline for comparison with previous years. 
Nick clarified that the data establishes a baseline for new processes and permitting systems, 
while historical data remains available for comparison. He noted that the existing CSRS system 
is outdated and lacks the capacity to support current reporting needs. 
 
4. Fran asked about staff adaptation to the new processes. Nick acknowledged a learning curve, 
including challenges with the rental registry technology. He said the Department is improving 
technology platforms and providing additional training and support to staf f. He noted that 
SAPHE 2.0 will help identify workforce training needs. 
 
5. Dr. Lowe requested clarification on the risk -based food licensing system. Commissioner 
Antanavica explained that establishments are categorized based on food type, preparation 
methods, establishment type, and compliance history. Lower-risk establishments receive fewer 
inspections, while higher-risk establishments may receive up to four annually. Risk categories, 
inspection frequency, and fees may change based on compliance history. 
 
6. Michael Perotto asked whether nail salons fall under the Department’s jurisdiction. Nick 
clarified that nail salons are regulated and licensed by the Commonwealth and are subject to 
state inspection. 
 
Upcoming Data Reporting Initiative 
Nick reported on ISD’s collaboration with DPH to improve inspection data collection and analysis. 
A digital reporting system now allows inspectors to document inspections, nuisance conditions, 
and code violations electronically. Preliminary findings on ins pection activity and trends are 
expected to be presented at the next Board meeting. 
 
The Board thanked ISD and DPH staff for their efforts in implementing the new processes and 
noted that improved data collection will support public health decision -making and program 
improvements The Chair thanked ISD staff for the update and their continued collaboration with 
DPH. 
 
9. Commissioner’s Report– Seema Dixit, HHS Commissioner  
Commissioner Seema Dixit thanked Commissioner Nick and Director Lee for presenting the data. 
She also highlighted the strong collaboration between DPH and ISD.  
- Commissioner Dixit provided an update on the Unhoused Committee, a monthly 
collaboration of organizations serving individuals experiencing homelessness. The group 
is developing a strategic framework focused on shelter capacity, outreach, service 
connections, and care coordination. Further updates will be provided as the work 
progresses. 
 
- Commissioner Dixit highlighted the City’s Community Resource Asset Mapping (CRAM) 
initiative, which identifies shelters, sober housing, social services, and other community 
resources. The resource identifies shelters, sober housing, social services, and other 
community support throughout the city. She noted that the goal is to develop the resource
into a live dashboard to help residents and service providers locate available  resources, 
including food pantries, shelters, temporary housing, and other supports.  CRAM is 
available through the City of Worcester Health and Human Services website. 
 
- Commissioner Dixit provided an update on Worcester’s opioid abatement funding, which 
comes from national pharmaceutical settlements and is distributed based on factors such as 
population and opioid-related impacts. Worcester has received annual funding since 2023, 
with allocations expected through 2039. 
 
- She announced an upcoming Opioid Stakeholders Meeting scheduled for August 19, 2026, 
intended to establish ongoing engagement with community partners and stakeholders. 
Discussion topics will include the use of opioid abatement funds, opioid overdose trends , 
reductions in overdose fatalities compared with state and national data, evidence -based 
practices, and strategies for future prevention efforts. The information gathered will help 
inform future priorities and potential requests for proposals related to o pioid prevention 
and overdose response.  She encouraged Board members and interested parties to 
participate in the stakeholder meeting due to the importance of opioid prevention as a 
public health issue. This will be held August 19, 2026 
 
- Commissioner Dixit announced an International Overdose Awareness Day event at City 
Hall on August 31, 2026. The event will honor lives lost to opioid overdose and include 
public health data, a moment of silence, and remarks from individuals with lived 
experience. 
 
- Commissioner Dixit provided an update on the Division of Youth Opportunities’ summer 
camp program, which runs for six weeks from July through mid -August and is serving 
approximately 480 youth ages 7 –12. This is an annual initiative supporting Worcester 
youth. 
 
10. Community HealthLink Update on closing 
- The Commissioner reported that DPH continues to receive updates from community 
partners regarding healthcare access concerns. The Department is participating in 
coordination efforts to connect residents at risk of losing coverage with available resources, 
including pro bono legal assistance. She explained that while DPH is not directly leading 
this effort, the Department continues to participate in coordination calls and remains 
informed. 
 
Board questions 
Board member Michael Perotto asked about the impact of the Community HealthLink merger on 
employees and services. Commissioner Dixit reported that the merger has resulted in some staff 
reductions and voluntary departures due to organizational uncertainty. She noted that DPH 
continues to monitor the situation and the impact on caregivers and service providers.  Michael 
requested additional information on the CHL transition, including staffing, service continuity, and 
affected programs. Commissioner Dixit noted that the Board could request an update from CHL
leadership and that she had discussed having the CHL President attend a future Board meeting. 
She suggested an update may be more appropriate once the transition is finalized. 
 
Commissioner Dixit reported that she has been in communication with the acquiring organization, 
PHN, and expects representatives to address the Board after the transition to discuss services and 
plans. The Board emphasized the need for clarity on service continuity and the transfer of funding 
and state contracts. Commissioner Dixit explained that CHL notified the state of its planned 
closure and that the transition involves coordination with the state regarding contracts, programs, 
staffing, union matters, and regulatory requirements. 
 
Michael emphasized the importance of maintaining service continuity during the CHL transition 
and considering the impact on affected employees. He expressed hope that displaced CHL staff 
would be considered for available positions with successor organizations. 
 
Michael Perotto requested in the form of a motion, that the Board continue to receive Status update 
on Community Health Link and its ongoing transition. 
 
Michael Perotto moved that the Board receive updates on the status and transition of Community 
Health Link (CHL) and invite CHL leadership to a future Board meeting to discuss the transition, 
continuity of services, and its impact on clients and staff. 
 
The motion was approved by a unanimous vote. 
 
Patrick Lowe thanked staff for developing the community resource dashboard and noted its value 
for healthcare providers, particularly those assisting patients with social service and housing needs. 
He asked whether the dashboard would include details on available services. Commissioner Dixit 
explained that the dashboard currently provides some service information and is being enhanced 
while maintaining privacy requirements. She noted that sensitive resources, such as domestic 
violence shelters, cannot be publicly identified.  Staff are working with agencies to determine 
appropriate information to share and improve connections to services. 
 
Dr. Lowe asked about the administration of the City’s opioid abatement funding. Commissioner 
Dixit explained that the Health and Human Services Department receives and administers the 
funds on behalf of the City. She noted that she had not yet received the current  funding cycle but 
provided background on prior allocations. She reported that the previous funding round included 
nine mini-grants of approximately $50,000 each to community organizations. The grants supported 
opioid prevention and response efforts, including overdose prevention, Narcan distribution, harm 
reduction, shelter support, and other services. One grant supported Community Health Link’s 
mobile shower program for individuals experiencing homelessness. 
 
Commissioner Dixit reported that two larger grants were also awarded, including funding for a 
substance use treatment center that remains in development pending required processes and 
documentation. She noted that the August 19 stakeholder meeting will rev iew prior investments, 
progress, evidence -based practices, and future priorities to inform an RFP anticipated for late 
October or November. The meeting will be recorded, and materials will be shared with Board 
members unable to attend.
Concerns Regarding TPS and Immigration Impacts 
Fran raised concerns about potential changes to Temporary Protected Status (TPS) and their impact 
on Worcester residents, families, and essential workers. She asked about City plans to support 
affected residents and emphasized the need for community preparedness. She emphasized that the 
issue extends beyond individual cases, noting that many affected individuals are long -term 
Worcester residents who have lived, worked, and contributed to the community for years. She 
asked how City leadership plans to address the po tential impacts. Commissioner Dixit responded 
that the City and community partners have discussed available resources, including pro bono legal 
assistance. She noted that she did not have details on the City’s broader response plan but 
recognized the potential impact on the Worcester community  and the importance of addressing 
these potential impacts on vulnerable residents. 
 
Dr. Lowe noted that the issue could have broader community impacts, including disruptions to 
healthcare, social services, and other essential sectors, as well as effects on individuals and 
families.  
 
Dr. Lowe introduced a second motion. 
 
Dr. Lowe moved that Commissioner Seema Dixit, in collaboration with City administration and 
community partners, provide a future report  to the BOH on the City’s planning and response to 
potential community and public health impacts associated with changes to Temporary Protected 
Status (TPS). The report would include available information on preparedness, contingency 
planning, support for affected residents, and continuity of essential services. 
 
It was unanimously approved by the Board. 
 
The Chair noted that, as City Council is again considering the CRB issue, the Board should revisit 
its previous discussions and position from 2020 and 2021. 
Fran made a motion to include a discussion of the Civilian Review Board as an agenda item for 
the next Board meeting.  
 
The motion was approved unanimously with a (4–0). 
 
The Chair asked the Commissioner to obtain and distribute the 2020–2021 meeting minutes related 
to the CRB discussions. She said the Human Rights Commission had also been involved and may 
have previously taken a position. She suggested inviting the Human Rights Commission Chair to 
a future meeting to provide background and its current perspective. The Board agreed that this 
would be helpful. 
 
Mike Perotto raised a procedural question regarding the appointment of Human Rights 
Commission members and suggested confirming with the City Manager before inviting a 
representative to participate, noting its complexity and the City Council’s current discussions. He 
supported revisiting the Civilian Review Board.
The Chair requested a motion to communicate with the City Manager regarding the Board’s 
interest in revisiting the Civilian Review Board. 
 
The Chair moved that staff communicate with the City Manager to inform the Administration of 
the Board’s interest in engaging with the Human Rights Commission regarding the Civilian 
Review Board. The discussion would provide perspectives from other city boards and 
commissions as the Board revisits its prior position. 
 
The motion was unanimously approved. 
 
11.  Next Meeting Date & Topics 
Next Meeting: September 14, 2026 
Topics: 
• Update on the status and transition of Community Health Link. 
• Temporary Protected Status (TPS)R: The city’s plan and response to community and public 
health impacts associated with the changes.  
• Discussion regarding the Civilian Review Board (CRB). 
12.  Adjournment 
 
A motion to adjourn was made by Michael Perotto. The motion passed unanimously. 
 
The meeting adjourned at 8:00p.m. 
 
 
NB: The BOH meeting for September 14, 2026, was adjourned without 
deliberations due to technical difficulties. It is rescheduled for Wednesday, 
September 30, 2026, from 6:30pm-8:30pm.

3. Emerging Infectious Diseases: Update 
Ebola — Current Situation & Massachusetts Impact 
• The ongoing Ebola outbreak is in the Democratic Republic of Congo and 
Uganda, caused by the Bundibugyo strain. 
• No cases have been detected in the United States, and the CDC states the risk to 
the American public is very low. 
• Massachusetts impact: No cases, no specific travel-related alerts beyond general 
CDC guidance. 
• https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/index.html 
 
    Hantavirus — Current Situation & Massachusetts Impact 
• A recent cluster of Andes virus–related hantavirus occurred on an international 
cruise ship. 
• No U.S. cases of Andes hantavirus have been detected, and CDC declares risk to 
the public as extremely low.  
• Routine U.S. hantavirus (Sin Nombre–related) continues at low levels (24 cases 
nationally this year), none linked to MA.  
• Massachusetts impact: No known cases or exposures. 
• https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/media/pdfs/2026/05/Andes-Virus-Guidancet_May14.pdf 
 
    Cyclosporiasis Outbreak — Current Situation & Massachusetts Impact 
• The U.S. is experiencing a large multistate Cyclospora outbreak, with thousands 
of cases nationwide. 
• A major outbreak is tied to iceberg lettuce (Taylor Farms), which was distributed 
in Massachusetts. 
• Massachusetts reports normal seasonal levels (~18 cases early season), not 
showing a large surge like the Midwest, but recalled lettuce DID reach MA food 
service locations.  
• https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/investigation.html
4 
 
Egg Recall — Salmonella & Massachusetts Impact 
• Over 19 million eggs recalled due to Salmonella Enteritidis contamination, tied to 
Texas-based producers.  
• Distribution includes TX, OK, LA, AR, NM, MS, but NOT Massachusetts. 
• Massachusetts impact: No affected shipments reported; MA stores were not 
included in FDA recall distribution lists. 
• https://www.fda.gov/food/outbreaks-foodborne-illness/outbreak-investigation-salmonella-

Public Health Excellence for Capacity Building
Also, known as the Local Public Health in MA Cities with 
Populations over 150,000
This funding is designed to align the commission’s 
recommendations to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of 
local and regional public health and to increase capacity to meet 
established performance standards. 
Centered in equity, the Grant recipients receive funding and 
technical support including racial equity training and 
considerations, sustainability planning, networking opportunities, 
and connections to state and federal resources to help them reach 
their goals and the needs of their local communities.
